outcome: The Yang-Mills existence and mass gap problem remains unsolved and unaccepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute. Since January 2024 there has been a large proliferation of self-published preprints (arXiv, Zenodo, ResearchGate, SSRN, Preprints.org, academia.edu) claiming full or partial proofs; at least one (Agawa, March 2025) was posted and then retracted by its own author, and one arXiv submission (Jacobsen, May-June 2025) was withdrawn by arXiv administrators for failing content-quality standards. The single most substantive AI-related event is an April 2026 Zenodo report by a human author with three named AI systems as co-authors, describing an 'intensive campaign' using 'adversarial AI collaboration across three frontier models' to attack the problem; it produced some genuine partial mathematical constructions (e.g. a mass-gapped noncommutative 4D gauge theory, confinement at all couplings) but explicitly failed to prove the continuum mass gap and reframed the question rather than answering it. No expert digestion, journal acceptance, or Clay Institute recognition of any of this work exists.

ai.basis_quote: We report the results of an intensive campaign to prove the Yang-Mills mass gap --- one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems... using adversarial AI collaboration across three frontier models.

disputes.summary: Dozens of mutually inconsistent self-published preprints across Zenodo, arXiv, ResearchGate, SSRN, Preprints.org and academia.edu each independently claim a complete or 'unconditional' proof of the mass gap (e.g. Silva-Filho's Lean-4-certified 'Unconditional Trilogy', Toupin's celestial-holography proof, the withdrawn Jacobsen and Agawa preprints, and others using names like 'Darkon-Yang-Mills', 'Big Boot Gauge Theory', and 'Quantum Cell Theory'). None has been reviewed or endorsed by any recognized expert, journal, or the Clay Mathematics Institute; several show hallmarks of low-quality or AI-generated text, and Zenodo itself has reported being flooded with bot/AI-crawler traffic during this period.

summary: The problem itself has not moved: the Clay Mathematics Institute's own page and the current Wikipedia article both still describe it as unsolved, and no proof or partial result here has received expert digestion, journal acceptance, or prize recognition. What has changed since January 2024 is the surrounding landscape: a large and growing volume of unreviewed, mostly self-published 'proof' preprints appeared on Zenodo, arXiv, ResearchGate, SSRN, Preprints.org and academia.edu, several with titles claiming complete or 'unconditional' resolutions (e.g. a Lean-4-'certified' trilogy by Silva-Filho, September 2026; a celestial-holography proof by Toupin, January 2026), one of which (Agawa, March 2025) was retracted by its own author after readers mistook it for an established result, and one arXiv submission (Jacobsen, May-June 2025) was withdrawn by arXiv administrators for not meeting content-quality standards. None of these has been accepted or verified by any recognized expert or institution, so none qualifies as resolved, claimed, or even partial under the scope rule: they are unverified assertions, not results a careful expert would treat as changing the bullet. The one event worth recording under `event`/`ai_role` is the April 2026 Zenodo report authored by John Henry Watt together with three AI systems listed as co-authors (Claude Opus 4.6 Extended, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Grok 4.20), which explicitly describes 'adversarial AI collaboration across three frontier models' used to systematically attack the mass gap problem. This is the clearest primary-source account of AI systems doing mathematical work (not just checking or formatting) that I found anywhere in this space: the systems are credited with producing matrix-model, noncommutative-gauge-theory, and lattice arguments as part of the campaign. But the campaign's own conclusion is that it failed to prove the continuum mass gap - it hit 'a factor-of-23 discrepancy between lattice and continuum formulations' and pivoted to arguing the question itself is 'not a dynamical mystery... but a geometric fact', i.e. it reframed rather than solved the problem. I classified this as `status: progress` (an instructive incident, not a resolution of any part of the stated problem) and `ai_role: incident`, per the rule that an AI-driven claim that surfaces and does not survive scrutiny (here, self-reported non-resolution rather than a formal retraction) is `progress`/`incident` dated to the claim. I treated `no_change_found` as false because this AI campaign is itself a recordable event even though the underlying mathematical problem is unchanged.
competing_reading: One could argue the correct status is plain `open` with `no_change_found: true`, treating the Watt/Claude/Gemini/Grok Zenodo report as just more unreviewed noise indistinguishable from the dozens of crank preprints, on the grounds that it produced no result that survives scrutiny and was never meant as a serious claim of resolution. I chose `progress`/`incident` instead because, unlike the other preprints, this one does not claim success - its authors' own account is a documented, named AI-driven attempt with a legible failure mode, which is exactly the kind of 'instructive incident' the rules ask to be captured rather than treated as silence. A stricter reading might also fold Silva-Filho's Lean-4 'certified' trilogy into ai_role `generated`/`claimed` if formal verification alone were deemed sufficient, but the rules are explicit that a machine-checked certificate nobody has reviewed is at most `claimed`, and here there is no evidence any human expert has reviewed it, and no AI system is credited by the author with producing the mathematics (Lean 4 is used as a proof checker, which is `ai_role: none` territory even if it were credible) - so I left that preprint out of the AI event entirely and only noted it as a dispute.
what_would_settle_it: Any statement from the Clay Mathematics Institute acknowledging receipt or review of a submitted solution; any peer-reviewed journal publication or serious expert blog digestion (e.g. Terence Tao, a mathematical-physics survey) endorsing or seriously engaging with one of these preprints; or a later, non-retracted version of one of the AI-co-authored or Lean-verified claims that survives independent scrutiny.
